paragraphs: The first view to be taken of this part of the government concerns the qualifications of the electors and of the elected. The electors are to have the same qualifications as the electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures. The definition of the right of suffrage is very justly regarded as a fundamental article of republican government. It was therefore the duty of the Convention to define and establish this right in the Constitution. To have left it open to occasional regulation by Congress would have been improper, for the reason just mentioned. To have left it to the legislative discretion of the States would have been improper for the same reason, and for the additional reason that it would have made that branch of the federal government, which ought to be dependent on the people alone, too dependent on the State governments. To have reduced the different qualifications in the different States to one uniform rule would probably have been as dissatisfactory to some of the States as it would have been difficult for the Convention. The provision the Convention made therefore appears to be the best within its power to choose. It must be satisfactory to every State, because it conforms to the standard the State itself has already established, or may establish. It will be safe for the United States because, being fixed by the State constitutions, it cannot be altered by the State governments, and it cannot be feared that the people of the States will alter this part of their constitutions in such a way as to abridge the rights secured to them by the federal Constitution.

The qualifications of the elected are less carefully and properly defined by the State constitutions, and are at the same time more suited to uniformity. The Convention has therefore very properly considered and regulated them. A representative of the United States must be twenty-five years of age; must have been a citizen of the United States for seven years; must, at the time of his election, be an inhabitant of the State he is to represent; and, during the time of his service, must hold no office under the United States. Under these reasonable limitations, the door of this part of the federal government is open to merit of every description, whether native or adoptive, whether young or old, and without regard to poverty or wealth, or to any particular profession of religious faith.

The term for which the representatives are to be elected falls under a second view that may be taken of this branch. To decide whether this article is proper, two questions must be considered: first, whether biennial elections will, in this case, be safe; secondly, whether they are necessary or useful.

First. It is essential to liberty that the government in general should have a common interest with the people. It is therefore particularly essential that the branch under consideration should have an immediate dependence on the people and an intimate sympathy with them. Frequent elections are unquestionably the only policy by which this dependence and sympathy can be effectively secured. But what particular degree of frequency may be absolutely necessary for the purpose does not seem capable of any precise calculation, and must depend on a variety of circumstances connected with it. Let us consult experience, the guide that ought always to be followed whenever it can be found.

The scheme of representation, as a substitute for a meeting of the citizens in person, was at most very imperfectly known to ancient politics. It is therefore only in more modern times that we can expect instructive examples. And even here, to avoid a search too vague and wide-ranging, it will be proper to confine ourselves to the few examples that are best known and bear the greatest resemblance to our particular case. The first to which this description ought to be applied is the House of Commons in Great Britain. The history of this branch of the English Constitution before the date of Magna Charta is too obscure to teach anything. Its very existence has been questioned among students of political antiquities. The earliest records of later date prove that parliaments were to SIT only every year, not that they were to be ELECTED every year. And even these annual sessions were left so much to the monarch's discretion that, under various pretexts, very long and dangerous intermissions were often contrived by royal ambition. To remedy this grievance, a statute in the reign of Charles II provided that the intermissions should not be prolonged beyond three years. On the accession of William III, when a revolution took place in the government, the subject was taken up again still more seriously, and it was declared to be among the fundamental rights of the people that parliaments ought to be held FREQUENTLY. By another statute, passed a few years later in the same reign, the term "frequently," which had referred to the three-year period settled in the time of Charles II, is given a precise meaning, since it is expressly enacted that a new parliament shall be called within three years after the end of the former one. The last change, from three to seven years, is well known to have been introduced fairly early in the present century, under an alarm for the Hanoverian succession. From these facts it appears that the greatest frequency of elections ever deemed necessary in that kingdom for binding the representatives to their constituents does not exceed a return every three years. And suppose we argue from the degree of liberty retained even under septennial elections and all the other vicious ingredients in the parliamentary constitution. Then we cannot doubt that reducing the period from seven to three years, along with the other necessary reforms, would so far extend the influence of the people over their representatives as to satisfy us that biennial elections, under the federal system, cannot possibly endanger the necessary dependence of the House of Representatives on their constituents.

Elections in Ireland, until recently, were regulated entirely at the discretion of the crown, and were seldom repeated except on the accession of a new prince or some other contingent event. The parliament that began with George II was continued throughout his whole reign, a period of about thirty-five years. The only dependence of the representatives on the people consisted in the people's right to fill occasional vacancies by electing new members, and in the chance of some event that might produce a general new election. The ability of the Irish parliament to maintain the rights of its constituents, so far as the disposition might exist, was also extremely shackled by the crown's control over the subjects of its deliberation. Lately these shackles, if I am not mistaken, have been broken, and octennial parliaments have also been established. What effect this partial reform may produce must be left to further experience. The example of Ireland, viewed in this way, can throw but little light on the subject. As far as any conclusion can be drawn from it, it must be this: if the people of that country have been able, under all these disadvantages, to retain any liberty whatever, the advantage of biennial elections would secure to them every degree of liberty that might depend on a proper connection between their representatives and themselves.

Let us bring our inquiries nearer home. The example of these States when they were British colonies claims particular attention, though it is so well known that little needs to be said about it. The principle of representation, in one branch of the legislature at least, was established in all of them. But the periods of election were different. They varied from one to seven years. Have we any reason to infer, from the spirit and conduct of the representatives of the people before the Revolution, that biennial elections would have been dangerous to the public liberties? The spirit that showed itself everywhere at the beginning of the struggle, and that overcame the obstacles to independence, is the best of proofs that a sufficient portion of liberty had been enjoyed everywhere to inspire both a sense of its worth and a zeal for its proper enlargement. This remark holds good as much for the colonies whose elections were least frequent as for those whose elections were most frequent. Virginia was the colony that stood first in resisting the parliamentary usurpations of Great Britain; it was also the first to espouse, by public act, the resolution of independence. Yet in Virginia, if I have not been misinformed, elections under the former government were septennial. This particular example is brought into view not as a proof of any peculiar merit, for the priority in those instances was probably accidental. Still less is it brought as a proof of any advantage in SEPTENNIAL elections, for when compared with greater frequency they are inadmissible. It is offered merely as a proof, and I think a very substantial one, that the liberties of the people can be in no danger from BIENNIAL elections.

The conclusion resulting from these examples will be considerably strengthened by recalling three circumstances. The first is that the federal legislature will possess only a part of that supreme legislative authority that is vested completely in the British Parliament, and that, with a few exceptions, was exercised by the colonial assemblies and the Irish legislature. It is a received and well-founded maxim that, where no other circumstances affect the case, the greater the power is, the shorter its duration ought to be; and, conversely, the smaller the power, the more safely its duration may be extended. In the second place, it has been shown on another occasion that the federal legislature will not only be restrained by its dependence on its people, as other legislative bodies are, but will also be watched and controlled by the collateral legislatures of the individual States, which other legislative bodies are not. And in the third place, no comparison can be made between the means that the more permanent branches of the federal government will have for seducing the House of Representatives from its duty to the people, if they should be disposed to seduce it, and the means of influence over the popular branch possessed by the other branches of the governments cited above. With less power to abuse, therefore, the federal representatives can be less tempted on one side, and will be doubly watched on the other.
